name: Thornburg Village (Normandy Village)

dates.altered: Expanded once in 1928 and again in 1955, according to a walking-tour account read the same day; parking structures for residents are hidden from the street. Clio's entry says 'built in 1927 (with later additions)'.
dates.note: The style node's exemplar gives 1927 and every source read here agrees.

refs.title: Thornburg Village - Clio
refs.note: Gives the address as '1781-1851 Spruce Streeet' [sic] and says 'Thornburg Village is a City of Berkeley Landmark and was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1983.' Entry by Rebecca Woodham, citing Sam Whiting, 'Towers, Turrets, and More: Normandy Village evokes rural France--in Berkeley', sfgate.com, October 10, 2004.

refs.title: Thornburg Village - Berkeley, California - Atlas Obscura
refs.note: Says the buildings 'were designated a City of Berkeley Landmark in 1983' and are still occupied. It does NOT repeat the National Register claim.

refs.title: Thornburg Village (Normandy Village), Berkeley
refs.note: Locates the group at Spruce Street and Hearst Avenue, names Jack Wood Thornburg as its developer at twenty-five, describes the intended mix of 'French-Norman, Scandinavian and Mediterranean influences', and dates the Berkeley landmark designation to 1983 without mentioning a federal listing.

note: Written for WP-11.2 Tranche 2. UNRESOLVED, AND THE DISAGREEMENT IS RECORDED RATHER THAN SETTLED: one source says the village was added to the National Register in 1983 and two others say only that it became a City of Berkeley Landmark in that year. No National Register reference number was found on any surface, so no `nrhp` ref is written; the claim is quoted in the Clio ref's note where a later reader can test it. The style node names W. R. Yelland as architect and Jack Wood Thornburg as client; the sources read here agree, and the Berkeley designation - not a federal one - is the protection that can be cited today. WP-11.2 Tranche 2, Tudor/Jacobethan/storybook cluster: `storybook-style` now names this record too, rather than writing a second record for the same street. The two nodes are not in conflict about it -- storybook-style's own description says the idiom reached the Bay Area by the mid-1920s and the Los Angeles Times says the same, and french-normandy-revival's claim on the village is about its sources rather than its manner. Its name and location strings are unchanged and both exemplars print them identically.
